newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LEHMAN TO DEFEND TITLE IN CONFIDENT MOOD.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEHMAN TO DEFEND TITLE IN CONFIDENT MOOD.

text.p: Tom Lehman is leaving no stone unturned in his bid for a second successive British Open golf championship at Royal Troon this week.
Winning the Loch Lomond World Invitational against a tough field on Saturday was merely his latest step in a bid to emulate the last man to retain the title, fellow American Tom Watson in 1983.

Lehman had already decided earlier last week to forego this weekend's squad trip to September's Spanish Ryder Cup venue of Valderrama which several other U.S. team members made, including Tiger Woods.
"It would have been too chaotic with all the demands on me at Troon," he said. "I don't think (captain) Tom (Kite) is going to kick me off the team if I don't go."
Last year, just two months after capturing the trophy at Royal Lytham for his first major title, Lehman began planning this month's defence.
After finishing the European Open in Ireland last October, he flew to Scotland to play a round at Troon.
"Winning the Open was so magical I decided I wanted to do everything I could to win it again this time," he said.
Playing alone, he wrote down everything he noticed about the course.
Then he went off and organised his accommodation for this week for himself, his wife Melissa and their three children - all of whom were with him last week.
"I wanted to be sure I had done everything I could to make my stay over here as comfortable as possible so I could concentrate on what really matters - getting my head right for my defence," he said.
His five-stroke triumph on Saturday at the Loch Lomond course could not have gone better.

After opening with a six-under-par 65 to stand two shots off the lead, he took over at the top with a second-round 66 and closed with two 67s to finish five shots clear of U.S. Open champion Ernie Els.
"All parts of my game were clicking. Everything about my game was under control and solid," he said. "This has been a very fulfilling week of golf for me."
The only thing he could find to quibble about was that he missed a few short putts.
"But then I made some long ones," he said. "Golfers are never happy. They always think they could do better. But I'm not sure I can do a whole lot better.
"Going into a major always requires that you go in with confidence. I feel I am definitely on top of my game."
Only one thing has happened to disturb Lehman's preparations for the defence.
That was the day he went home from an event some months ago to discover his kids had broken the Auld Claret Jug -- the championship trophy.
"It had been on a mantle out of their reach but I came home to find it had been bent out of shape and sitting at a 15 degree angle.
"A decorator friend of my wife's had decided it looked better lower down at floor level and one of my kids had dropped it," he said.
It has since been repaired and was to arrive at Troon later on Sunday.
"I'm bring it back grudgingly. I'm reluctant to part with it," Lehman said.
